headline: High risk of prompt injection and cascading errors from ctx’s MCP/file observation into LangGraph’s writable, networked orchestration graph.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: ctx observes Claude Code PostToolUse/Stop events and uses MCP stdio, while LangGraph can wire developer-defined tools and run agent graphs. That creates a plausible content-to-instruction bridge if ctx output is fed into LangGraph nodes, but the exact bridge is not documented, so I avoid high.
conditions: IF ctx output is routed into a LangGraph node without provenance filtering
IF Claude Code event text is treated as instructions by downstream nodes
mitigations: Add a provenance tag to ctx outputs before passing them onward
Insert a prompt-injection filter on all ctx-derived text
Require a human review step before LangGraph executes ctx-derived instructions
Restrict LangGraph nodes to read-only parsing for ctx outputs

B_data_leakage.rationale: ctx touches filesystem, audit/runtime logs, graph data, and MCP servers; LangGraph reads and writes application-defined files and sends data to model providers. If they share a workspace or checkpointer, sensitive runtime data can flow from ctx into LangGraph and then to third-party APIs. The shared-workspace path is not explicit, so this is medium rather than high.
conditions: IF ctx and LangGraph share a filesystem, checkpointer, or log directory
IF LangGraph forwards ctx-derived state to model providers
mitigations: Separate ctx and LangGraph storage directories
Disable logging of ctx-derived secrets before LangGraph ingestion
Redact audit/runtime logs before any model-provider call
Use distinct credentials for each agent
Add a denylist for sensitive file paths in LangGraph

C_capability_conflict.rationale: ctx can install packages and use filesystem-backed MCP tooling, while LangGraph can execute shells, write/read files, spawn subprocesses, and use broad network egress. Both can mutate the same local resources, and LangGraph explicitly supports shared state across instances; without locking, concurrent writes can corrupt state or overwrite each other.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same directory or checkpointer
IF ctx package installation or MCP hooks run concurrently with LangGraph file writes
mitigations: Assign separate working directories
Serialize writes with a lock file
Disable package installation in ctx during shared runs
Use per-agent checkpointer namespaces
Run both agents under separate OS users

D_cascading_error.rationale: ctx is designed to observe Claude Code events, so its outputs are likely to be treated as operational context; LangGraph then orchestrates tool-using nodes that may act on that context. If LangGraph consumes ctx output without verification, a mistaken or malicious ctx summary can cascade into downstream actions or incorrect state updates.
conditions: IF LangGraph uses ctx summaries as authoritative inputs
IF downstream LangGraph nodes trigger tool calls or external API actions
mitigations: Require schema validation on ctx outputs
Add a verification node before any action-taking node
Log and diff ctx claims against source artifacts
Limit downstream nodes to advisory mode until reviewed

E_compliance.rationale: ctx explicitly touches audit/runtime logs and graph data, while LangGraph handles model-provider API keys and can persist graph state via checkpointers. If regulated or sensitive data enters the shared graph, retention and residency obligations can diverge between the two systems. The profiles do not specify a concrete jurisdiction mismatch, so medium is the highest supportable level.
conditions: IF regulated data is stored in ctx logs or LangGraph checkpointer state
IF retention or deletion requests must cover both systems
mitigations: Document a shared retention policy
Exclude regulated data from ctx logs
Set a deletion workflow for LangGraph checkpointer entries
Store secrets only in a dedicated secret manager
Review residency of any external model-provider calls
